name: Neck training (flexion/extension)

lead: Neck training means working the neck forward and backward against resistance. Users do it for a thicker, stronger neck that they say complements the jaw, improves posture and gives a more masculine frame.

Resistance exercise loads the neck flexor and extensor muscles. Trials have studied it in other settings: randomized trials in women with chronic neck pain compared strength and endurance training, a pilot trial tested a six-week program in under-19 rugby players, and a systematic review addressed neck training to reduce head acceleration events in sport. No study has examined it for appearance.

paras: People use towels, hands, plates or machines for forward and backward neck work, usually as a regular part of a lifting routine with gradual progression, and results in size build over months like other muscle training.
No harms were documented in the sources used; forum members raise questions about soreness, asymmetry and sleep apnea without published backing.

chain: More masculine neck, jaw and frame
angle.text: Training the neck forward and back with towels, hands, plates or machines loads the neck muscles, building a thicker, stronger neck that users say complements the jaw, posture and physique. Neck training is studied for pain and sport performance.

lead: Neck training in the flexion and extension sense means exercising the neck forward and backward against resistance, often with a towel, hands, plate or machine. In looksmaxxing forums it is promoted as a way to build a thicker, stronger neck that proponents say complements the jaw, physique and posture [1][2]. The neck's most visible muscles, the sternocleidomastoid on each side and the trapezius that shapes the slope into the shoulders, are the ones that give the neck its outline [3][4].

Proponents describe a chain: stronger, thicker neck muscles give a wider base under the jaw, a more balanced head-to-shoulder proportion and an upright head position, so the face reads as better supported [1][5]. Forum members also pair neck work with jaw and posture routines [5][2].

Published research on neck training mostly addresses chronic neck pain and injury reduction in sport, not appearance. Randomized trials in women with chronic neck pain compared high-intensity strength and endurance training [6], a pilot trial tested a tailored six-week program in under-19 rugby players [7], and a systematic review and Delphi study addressed neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in sport [8]. No study found examined neck training for cosmetic purposes.
infobox: Sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, splenius and deep neck flexors [3][4]
Thicker neck, stronger look, more upright head carriage [1]
Chronic neck pain, sport head-impact exposure [6][7][8]
Contact sports such as rugby, American football and wrestling [7][19]
Pain and sport-injury research; none for appearance

paras: The neck connects the head to the trunk through muscles attached to the skull, hyoid bone, clavicles and sternum [3]. The sternocleidomastoid runs obliquely across the side of the neck from the sternum and collarbone to the skull behind the ear; it is among the largest and most superficial neck muscles and is easy to see when the head turns [4]. Acting together, the two sternocleidomastoids flex the neck and extend the head, and acting alone one turns the head to the opposite side [4]. The trapezius bounds the back of the neck and shapes the slope from neck to shoulder [3].

Forward and backward movements load the flexors at the front, including the sternocleidomastoids and deeper muscles, and the extensors at the back [4]. An MRI study of ten adult men and ten ten-year-old boys fitted a power-law relationship between neck circumference and the cross-sectional area of six neck muscle groups, giving a way to relate the outer measurement of the neck to the muscle inside it [9]. Wikipedia attributes the larger average neck circumference of men mainly to muscle mass and body composition [3].

Forum guides describe the two core movements as a forward curl that works the front of the neck and a backward extension that works the back, often with a towel over the head for comfort [1]. People use a towel, their own hands for resistance, a weight plate, a head harness, or a neck machine, and some also include side movements [1][10]. In a reply to that guide, one member said slow, stretch-focused repetitions can work without added weight [1].

Neck work in sport is established in contact and combat sports. A randomized pilot trial in 34 male rugby players aged 16 to 18 used a tailored six-week neck conditioning program [7]. A 2021 systematic review of strength and conditioning protocols for neck strength found three studies, all in male athletes, two of which reported significant gains in isometric neck strength; the authors concluded evidence was insufficient to say that strengthening reduces impact injury risk in adult sport [11].

Members commonly discuss neck work alongside jaw and posture routines. Forum thread titles include a post arguing that neck training is needed for people who have built a wider face or sharper jawline but still have a thin neck, an advice thread on high versus low repetitions, and threads of progress photos [5][12][13]. Forward head posture, which Wikipedia describes as the head sitting forward of the shoulders with the chin jutting forward, is a recurring concern, and its suggested exercises include strengthening the deep front neck muscles and shoulder-blade retractors [14].

A randomized study of 180 women with chronic neck pain assigned participants to high-intensity strength training, local muscle endurance training or a control group, and evaluated changes in neck strength, pain and disability, with a one-year follow-up [6]. Wikipedia reports that strengthening exercises may improve function and pain in neck pain and that craniocervical flexion exercises are reported as effective for chronic neck pain without a specific cause, adding that the wording of the evidence is tentative in places [15]. Other work has explored how experimental neck pain and training affect motor cortex excitability [16][17][18].

A 2014 study measured neck strength and circumference in 6,704 US high school athletes across 51 schools and followed them for concussion; smaller neck circumference and weaker neck strength were associated with concussion, and each extra pound of neck strength was associated with 5% lower odds of concussion after adjustment [19]. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of eight studies with 7,625 participants found that five studies linked greater neck strength or motor control to lower concussion incidence, but pooled effects were small and non-significant with very low certainty of evidence [20]. A prospective cohort of 136 professional rugby players found that neck strength did not predict concussion in a clinically meaningful way [21]. A 2023 analysis examined injury-reduction programs containing neuromuscular neck exercises and soccer head and neck injuries [22], and a 2025 systematic review and Delphi consensus study addressed neck training to reduce head acceleration events [8]. A pilot study evaluated a neuromuscular neck training device for multiplanar neck strength [23].

Because neck circumference is easy to measure, it has been studied as a health marker. In 1,912 Turkish adults, neck circumference averaged 36.7 cm, and each one-standard-deviation increase was associated with metabolic syndrome and with obstructive sleep apnea [24]. In 3,942 sleep clinic patients, neck-to-height ratio was the strongest predictor of apnea severity, explaining 19% of its variability [25]. These studies measure total neck size, which includes fat as well as muscle, and do not address muscle growth from training. A 2014 case report described a 37-year-old man with weightlifting-related neck muscle hypertrophy who developed head-turn-triggered near-fainting from vertebral artery occlusion; the authors discussed whether muscle bulk might affect vertebral artery flow [26].

A forum guide presents neck exercises as giving a thicker, stronger neck that goes with the physique, could improve posture and a 'high T' look [1]. Other threads ask about frequency and repetitions, whether training one side more would cause asymmetry, and why months of training showed no visible change [10][27]. A 2019 thread titled around sleep apnea indicates that members also discuss possible airway concerns [28].

Thread titles on looksmax.org also ask for 'neck training for better looks', share before-and-after neck photos and compare routines [2][5][2]. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article places such practices among the milder softmaxxing and fitness end of the scene, as distinct from surgical or unconventional routes [29].
No studies found on neck flexion and extension training for cosmetic appearance. Trials exist for chronic neck pain [6] and for sport populations [7][8][22], but they do not measure looks.

lore.intro: Neck training is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, discussed as a way to improve overall look and sometimes as a complement to jaw work [1][2][5].
